utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I please introduce Mr. Trajce Gjorgjiev who has been working with my team. He is from Macedonia and has been of invaluable assistance to us these past many months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, the Chamber issued its decision on the Prosecution motion to exclude evidence of Angelina Pikulic, and it will now issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution's motion to exclude in part the evidence of Witness Branislav Dukic and the Prosecution's motion to exclude in part the evidence of Witness Radojka Pandurevic, both filed on the 21st of November, 2012. I will refer to those two motions as the Dukic motion and the Pandurevic motion, respectively. In the Dukic and Pandurevic motions, the Prosecution requests that certain portions of the proposed Rule 92 ter statements of these two witnesses be excluded as they are irrelevant to the charges in the indictment in that they pertain to crimes committed against Serbs. The accused responded on the 26th of November, 2012, opposing both the Dukic and Pandurevic motions. In relation to the Dukic motion, the accused argues that Dukic's statement contains relevant evidence regarding the locations, conduct, and movement of the ABiH, which are live issues in this case. With respect to the Pandurevic motion, the accused argues that Pandurevic's statement includes evidence that pertains to the take-over of Hadzici municipality and rebuts adjudicated facts which judicial notice was taken in this case. Furthermore, in relation to both motions, the accused argues that evidence concerning the mistreatment of Serbs in Sarajevo is relevant to show why the VRS would want to target ABiH forces that were committing crimes against Bosnian Serbs and explain why some individual Serbs may have committed crimes out of rage or revenge. As a preliminary matter, the Chamber reminds both parties once again of the utmost importance of filing witness-related motions in a timely manner. The Chamber notes that the Pandurevic motion was filed over three weeks after the accused filed his Rule 92 ter notification for Pandurevic and that this witness is scheduled to testify this week. As is the case for the accused, the Chamber expects the Prosecution to file its witness-related motions sufficiently in advance so that the accused can respond and the Chamber can rule on the said motions prior to the witness's arrival in The Hague. Turning first to the Dukic motion, the Chamber notes that Dukic's proposed 92 ter statement is concerned, almost entirely, with detailed descriptions of crimes committed against the Serbs and against Dukic in particular. It also contains some references to previous meetings between Dukic and the Prosecution. As such, the Chamber considers that Dukic's evidence is not relevant to the charges in the indictment. While his statement does contain some remote references to the positions and military activity of the ABiH and the Bosnian Croat forces in and around Sarajevo, these are not only minimal but also general in nature and thus are not sufficient in and of themselves to warrant admitting parts of his statement. Accordingly, the Chamber decides, proprio motu, to exclude the evidence of Branislav Dukic in its entirety. With regard to the Pandurevic motion, the Chamber finds that paragraphs 1 to 12, 55, 56, 61 to 63, 65 and 66 of Pandurevic's Rule 92 ter statement are of relevance to the charges in the indictment. The remainder of her statement, however, is comprised of tu quoque or otherwise irrelevant evidence and will therefore not be admitted. Because Pandurevic's Rule 92 ter statement remains comprehensible even if the irrelevant portions are redacted, the Chamber orders the accused to redact the statement and remove the irrelevant paragraphs. Accordingly, the Chamber grants the Pandurevic motion in part and excludes paragraphs 13 to 54, 57 to 60, 64, and 67 of Pandurevic's witness statement and the associated exhibits therein. The Chamber allows the accused to tender the remainder of Pandurevic's statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter should the accused still wish to call Pandurevic to testify in this trial. In addition, in relation to the accused's argument as to the relevance of the tu quoque evidence in Pandurevic and Dukic Rule 92 ter statements, namely that it will explain why the VRS targeted ABiH forces and why some individual Serbs may have committed crimes in revenge, the Chamber wishes to make it clear that the accused is not charged with targeting ABiH forces but with targeting civilians. Furthermore, the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is clear, starting with the Tadic appeal judgement, that personal motives of physical perpetrators of crimes such as revenge, for example, are not relevant to determining the responsibility of the accused. Accordingly, since the tu quoque evidence offered here is not relevant to the responsibility of the accused as alleged in the indictment, the Chamber will not allow him to introduce detailed and comprehensive evidence of such nature under the guise of relevance to this trial. The Chamber urges Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Robinson to bear this in mind. Having said that, could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I say something for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, I have to express my disappointment, because I am being accused here for spreading fear amongst the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we will not entertain your statement with respect to your disappointment with the Court's ruling. The Court has issued its ruling, and there's other steps to take on your part if you're not satisfied with its ruling. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the Court's reminder concerning the timeliest possible notice about witness-related matters, I wanted to bring, therefore, to the Court's attention the matter that can be considered hot off the presses. Last night at 9.00 p.m. we received copies of the signed statement of KDZ318, who was due to give evidence tomorrow morning. Earlier in that day the Chamber had limited the cross-examination of this witness to one hour. In this new statement we now find 11 paragraphs of new evidence, some of which, as it happens, relates to the testimony of a witness about to take the stand. It refers to 11 new associated exhibits that were not mentioned in the original notification, the 92 ter notification on October 30th, and none of which are on the Defence 65 ter list, and five of which are not translated. Despite repeated warnings to Dr. Karadzic and his associates about the extent of last minute changes to statements, the practice continues, and this kind of late notice of new material is manifestly unfair and obviously and directly affects the Prosecution's capacity to effectively prepare for cross-examination. Under these circumstances, we would urge that any new information of that sort be led live and that the Prosecution -- that the cross-examination of the witness be held over so the Prosecution can prepare adequately -- for the Prosecution and furthermore, obviously that any untranslated documents not be permitted to be used under these circumstances. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will look into the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I may, I'm sorry to -- there is one additional matter I wanted to raise today. I had alluded to it earlier. I don't want to raise it now because it's a relatively lengthy submission. I don't mean a matter of a half hour or so, nothing of that nature, but I think it would be better if I raise it at the beginning of the next session so I wanted to alert the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you would you like to add anything to this, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there any reason for you to make that submission at the next session, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the Court wishes I can make it now, Mr. President, if that's what you're suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this concerns a matter that has been raised by now repeatedly. The Chamber will recall that at the 28 September Status Conference we first raised our concern about the Defence failure to provide adequate summaries, factual summaries, pursuant to Rule 65 ter(G). Now, at that time we advised the Court that rather than demand an immediate enforcement of the Rules and a Rule in particular which is designed to ensure both the fairness and efficiency of the proceedings, we were willing to work with and had been working with the accused and his staff toward a workable solution and to try to be as accommodating and flexible as possible, and we mentioned in particular our willingness to accept statements in lieu of 65 ter summaries, especially in the context of a case that's heavily dependent on 92 ter so that that would obviate any unnecessary work for the Defence. We came back to the Court on October 15th, the Pre-Trial Conference, and advised that despite our efforts, there was no success in the attempt to reach a workable solution. We told the Court about the hundreds of witnesses for whom there was neither a statement nor an adequate factual summary. We identified for the Trial Chamber the nature of some of the so-called summaries, including things along the lines of significant senior figures in the military or the police who we were advised would testify about their roles and activities regarding Srebrenica and its aftermath, obviously wholly topical and useless description of the fact that the witness will testify about a particular -- in the context of a particular component or the 90 separate municipality witnesses who were expected to "explain why some Muslims preferred to leave the municipality" or the many cut-and-paste summaries where the name of one municipality was substituted for another because the sweeping generalisations provided would work as well in one municipality as another. We told the Court that the situation was neither acceptable nor workable, and despite our efforts, we had been told that we could not expect to receive summaries even past the first quarter of the next year, and as we explained that means we would be operating in the dark and were operating in the dark with respect to the municipalities, the Srebrenica component and the hostage component. We told the Court at that time that we needed dead-lines. The Court -- and we suggested some specific dead-lines, in fact. The Court urged us again to go back to the accused and try to do what we could to work out some compromise solution, and we did just that. We went back. In fact, we took up on a suggestion that the Trial Chamber had made which I think was made at page 28839 of the Pre-Trial Conference where the Court suggested going back to the witness list and seeing if there are some witnesses that the Defence team already knows it would not be calling, and we sought as at least a preliminary matter the provision of some kind of A and B list or will call or won't call list so we could at least begin to assess the magnitude of the problem in light of a more realistic assessment of that list. That -- there was a delay in providing that, but when we finally got it, it quickly became apparent that that list was useless. We quickly found people who had been on the so-called B list, that is the less likely to be called list, appearing on the list of people soon to be called, and we found people who had been on the A list who were dropped completely from the case. So it became clear to us, and it's been acknowledged by the Defence, that that was not a useful list and provided us with no further insights or opportunities to craft an appropriate compromise. So I'm back today to seek dead-lines. And I need to emphasise, Mr. President, that this is not a failure of negotiation; it is instead a failure by the Defence to complete the tasks envisioned by the Rules and required by the Rules that would allow a reasonable and even generous compromise to take place. The Rules obviously envision that when -- when a party assembles its witness list it goes out, it identifies witnesses, it then goes out to find out what relevant information those witnesses may or may not have, and then in some fashion, usually through a factual summary as contemplated by 65 ter(G), it transmits that information to the other party and to the Court sufficiently in advance so that the integrity of the proceedings and the efficiency of the proceedings are not impaired. And instead of complying with that Rule, it appears that the Defence instead went out, identified witnesses, and then instead of perfecting that process as the Rules contemplate, it simply threw that name on a list and went out to find more witnesses. And so what we have is a list -- a lengthy, bloated, excessive list of people, many of whom the Defence has not only failed to identify what relevant information they have but has failed to communicate with at all. As Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff mentioned to Mr. Robinson during the course of our discussions, this is not a witness list. This is a wish list. It's only the image of a witness list. So instead of operating within the meaning of the Rules and the spirit of the Rules at a time when that was provided, the Defence used that time to simply assemble the largest possible witness list and now is -- is trying to do the work it should have done earlier at the expense of the Prosecution and indeed the Court. So we don't have the information we're entitled to have months after we were entitled to have it, which has manifold effects. We can't do the preparation, research or investigation that would otherwise be possible. We can't identify recurring themes and make assignments in a rational and efficient way. We can't identify the extent to which witnesses contradict each other. There are a myriad ways in which we are handicapped and unfairly prejudiced by the practice that the Defence has introduced, and indeed it's a reflection of what the Court alluded to at page 28827 of the Pre-Trial Conference: "We are at this point very concerned that you and your legal team appear to be openly disregarding all the rules and practices established and followed during the Prosecution case." Mr. President, under these circumstances, we continue to operate in the dark with respect to the municipality, Srebrenica, and hostage components. We can't begin under these circumstances. It's extremely unfair, and we need the concrete dead-lines we proposed earlier. We had previously proposed November and December. That was about a month ago. That means November -- that meant November for completion of the municipalities component and December for completion. That means getting all the statements in or summaries in - and I'll speak about that in just a second - by the end of those particular months. So now that would mean completion of the municipalities and the hostages component, information and provision of that information by the end of December, and Srebrenica by the end of January. Now, again we don't insist on a needless formality; that is the Defence goes out and gets statements and then spends additional time transforming that information into a 65 ter summary. Obviously this is a 92 ter case. The Defence has to go out now and meet the witnesses and get the information that they failed to get earlier. That's -- they need to do that in the form of statements. There is no reason to do it twice. They should simply get it in the form of a statement or draft statement as they've been doing and transmit that to the Prosecution and to the Court. Now, as mentioned, we spoke to Mr. Robinson in the context of our efforts to reach some workable mutual accord. He suggested that the Defence's working -- the Defence won't be able to do it because their prioritising one component at a time and only staying so far ahead. What we said in response I'll say to the Court as well, and that is that presumes the deployment of their resources to a -- toward a fixed objective, and that is the completion of all the 65 ter summaries or in this case all the statements for a witness list that has been repeatedly identified as excessive, as containing witnesses who provide irrelevant, marginal, or manifestly needlessly cumulative information and that's been alluded to by the Court on a number of occasions. If the Defence finally undertook a realistic appraisal of the witness list and focused on the witnesses who are most needed, then, in our submission -- and deployed their resources appropriately, the kind of obstacles that they have insisted prevent their compliance with the Rules of this Court would dissipate. In any event, the Court cannot permit this flouting of the Rules which has now gone on for an excessive -- well, been excessive for quite a while, but this now threatens to further affect the Prosecution's ability to prepare for witnesses as it is entitled to do. We struggled through the Sarajevo component. That was a bit different because the Defence had front loaded it slightly but during the process we learned what an adverse impact it can have on our ability to prepare for their remaining components and that's why I'm before the Court today and now advising the Court that no compromise solution has been reached or appears possible and dead-lines need to be imposed. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was listening to French translation. Yes, Mr. Tieger. To be clear, what are the specific remedies you are seeking that is to be done within the respective dead-line again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The submission of, in this case, statements for the witnesses who are to be called for the municipalities and hostage component by the end of December, and the submission of statements for witnesses who are to be called for the Srebrenica component by the end of January, and in the event that -- for witnesses who now appear on the list and statements are not provided, those witness are considered to be no longer on the list because the Rules have not been complied with. And if the Defence later wants to -- seeks to add them to the list for good cause obviously the Rules provide for that possibility if good cause exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what about the summaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the Rules obviously -- excuse me. Excuse me, Mr. President. The 65 ter(G) refers to summaries, but we are operating in a 92 ter environment, so knowing that the Defence has to prepare the 92 ter statements, it's not our intention to make them prepare the statements as they will be doing and then spend additional time converting those into summaries. So the statements will suffice in lieu of the summaries, and we've been clear on that with them from the outset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Robinson. Would you like to respond? Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. I'm waiting for the interpretation to finish. I'm grateful to Mr. Tieger for having raised the topic, but I would like to remind you that I have prepared tens of witnesses that the Prosecution gave up on and also some municipalities that were dropped from the indictment at a later stage. That is one thing. Secondly, I would like to remind you of over 100 cases of violation of Rule 68. Also, I would like to remind you that during the Prosecution case, we had only two investigators who were supposed to match the years' long investigation carried out by the Prosecution. We come from a system that involves investigating judges who carry out an investigation for both sides. Here we are helpless. There is no way we can conduct the kind of investigation that the Prosecution had conducted. Secondly, we haven't been given enough time. Our modest request was to start in March, and that was very restrictive too. Further on, if you look at all the resources they had, primarily all the human resources they had, and if you look at what we have, although many people work for my Defence free of charge, pro bono, and they can barely keep up with the tempo. We will be examining two or three witnesses a day, after all, so it is absolutely impossible for us to meet any dead-lines in this situation without new people and possibly more time. Also, when the Prosecution was in a similar situation, they were given certain breaks, and they could prepare. That is what I know. Those are the facts. That is what we're grappling with. Maybe Mr. Robinson can add something from a legal point of view, but, Your Honours, there is no way of conducting a trial that would be fair for us, us who come from a different system where a proper and fair investigation is carried out on behalf of both parties before the trial actually commences. If our requests are not met, a shadow of doubt will be cast on the legality of the proceedings and the Tribunal itself. Perhaps Mr. Robinson can add something to that. Anyway, may I conclude by saying that we are falling on our face. We are working so hard, all of us. All of those who are working pro bono are also falling off their feet, but there is such a lot of work, and there are many details involved. There are a lot of adjudicated facts and so on and so forth. So if we see, for example, that a witness is denying an adjudicated fact, then we are not going to dwell on the matter; then we have to deal with the same matter with another witness, but that takes time. If the Trial Chamber accepts these dead-lines that we're going to ask for certain breaks, it would be a great pity indeed if these proceedings were to be unfair or incomplete. Could Mr. Robinson please say something from a legal point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, I want to say that we have done everything possible to work with the Prosecution to give them as much information as we have concerning the testimony of the people that we want to call as witnesses. So we have now disclosed some 160 statements in e-court which are available to the Prosecution at the rate of about 25 witnesses for the first month, and I expect it will pick up a little bit now that the times for cross-examination will be shortened, but that's six months or more worth of advanced notice of what exactly the witness will say in court since we hardly ever elicit any additional information from the witness. So we also tried to give the Prosecution disclosure of everything that we have concerning these witnesses. It's essentially an open file disclosure policy. The problem is that we don't have more information about what some of these witnesses are going to say until we interview them. We could provide a summary that's of greater detail as required by the Rule if some of those are deficient, but even as the Prosecution recognises, to do that will essentially be speculating or guessing or imagining what these witnesses would say unless we've actually had the opportunity to interview them and take a statement from them, and that wouldn't be of value to anyone and would just use up the very limited resources that we have. But if there's been a failure under Rule 65 ter to provide an adequate summary in any particular case, I would urge on the Prosecution to file a motion to identify the particular witness number and we will do our best to enhance the summary if that's what is required to comply with what the Prosecution feels it needs. But as a practical matter, we simply don't have the resources to take statements from all of the witnesses that we intend to call by the end of December or by the end of January, and if there's been one principle that the Prosecution has made very successful -- very successfully advocated before this Chamber, it is that evidence is not excluded when there is a delay in disclosure, and so to ask us to face the sanction of excluding evidence for which we have been unable to have an investigator take a statement from a witness by the end of December or the end of January is really not very practical and certainly not reciprocal when you take into account over 400 statements that the Prosecution failed to disclose to us during the -- by the dead-line it was given, for which not a single piece of evidence was ever excluded, or the thousands of Rule 68 documents which the Prosecution failed to provide with -- within the time required by Rule 68 for which not a single document was ever excluded. So I think it's better for the Prosecution and the Chamber and us to continue to try to work together with the limited resources that we have to do the maximum, to give the Prosecution as much notice as we can of evidence, and if they're disadvantaged by late notice, then the Chamber can employ the remedy which it did in our case, which is to postpone the cross-examination of the witness or maybe even postpone their appearance as a result of any prejudice caused to the Prosecution. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you like to add anything, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just -- only -- there are many things I could go into. I think the Court can probably take the comments on board and assimilate them, but I can't help but note that there's not even a shred of acknowledgement of what the Court has alluded to previously and that is the nature of this witness list and its manifestly excessive nature and the impact it has on this very problem. Instead -- instead the discussion is, again as it was when we were talking to Mr. Robinson, assuming that the Defence resources are being deployed against an intractable and fixed obstacle or issue and that is the witness list and the attempt to provide information pursuant to the Rules for all of these witnesses. In many respects, it gets back to the original decision by the Defence to assemble an extremely unrealistic so-called witness list in contravention of the Rules, one that has been recognised by the Court to be unrealistic on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will take this issue under advisement and issue a ruling in due course. Unless there are any other matters, we'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Just an administrative matter from yesterday. When we ended with the witness we were speaking about document 65 ter 09365. I would like to ask that that be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6005, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dunjic. I apologise for your inconvenience. There were matters to deal with on the part of the Trial Chamber. Once the witness is in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to note that the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Lattanzi being away due to her urgent personal matters. Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have 65 ter 24201, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dunjic. Yesterday when we broke --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yesterday when we concluded, we had just been speaking about the arrests that took place in December of 1992, and early on in your cross-examination you had conceded that you were dismissed from the VRS in January of 1993 and that dismissal was involuntary. I'd like to focus in on that. Sir, isn't it true that in the middle of January you were told by Commander Galic that by January 26 you were going to be -- you were going to have to leave and your contract would not be extended?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But as we saw in the last document from yesterday, wasn't it true that by the end of December -- or excuse me, by December 16, the day after the arrests, the SRK was already considering your dismissal?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, whether they considered that after I left, I don't know, but the document that was shown to me yesterday is a document in which the colonel I arrested proposes those measures. That is that. It's not about the decision or meeting in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dunjic, isn't it correct that between August -- excuse me, September of 1992 when you joined the Igman Brigade and January of 1993 when you were dismissed, that Brne and his paramilitary unit were never meaningfully under the command of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let us clarify something. I was appointed commander of the Igman Brigade. I did not just join it. That was my first point. Secondly, although I find you highly likable, you cannot -- you cannot suggest to me that although according to Galic's statement there were 1 per cent or according to my statements there were 3 per cent of volunteers, and you are ignoring the ruling of the Supreme Court. According to the ruling of the Supreme Court, they lost the attribute to volunteers. They joined the military, and they're not paramilitaries therefore. I commanded thousands of men, and I did not focus on those units. I did not focus on that unit only. That was minor compared to the total manpower. I had other problems there as well. I mentioned in the beginning that I was the only professional soldier in the unit. According to your documents, according to the documents you have, you saw in my statement that there was fighting every day, that there was shelling every day. And yesterday I also omitted to tell you when you asked me about the conversation with Prstojevic, most of the conversations that we had had to do with the shelling of the transformer station at Vrelo Bosne, the destruction of that station which was later destroyed. Anyway, the focus of my work was defence, defence from everyday attacks, care for civilians and even care for civilians on the other side, if you will, in relation to the transformer station and the cuts in water supplies, but this unit was a volunteer unit, not a paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And again, for the fourth time you've brought up the Supreme Court decision and we'll get into that, but at the moment we're talking about your dismissal. Now, we're going to look at the document before us and this is dated 18 January, but it speaks about an event that happened on the 14th of January, and it talks about an incident that occurred in your apartment between members of military police and Brne's Chetniks, and it says - and this is a MUP document - We have learned on that day the commander of the SRK Corps, Galic, gave a cocktail party at a hotel in order to celebrate his promotion to the rank of general and on which occasion he informed you to leave your command post on January 26 and that the corps will not extend your contract. Sir, this in fact did happen; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] go ahead. I'm sorry. You said?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. First of all, that's not the way correspondence evolves in the military. My superior officer does not say you're going to stay until then and then you're not going to be there. This is done in writing. Secondly, I did not come to the Army of Republika Srpska on the basis of some contract. I came on the basis of an order, and I can leave the army on the basis of an order and those were the rules that were in force in the Army of Republika Srpska and in the JNA as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. But let's go on to what happened after the party. And following the end of the ceremony, Major Dunjic invited General Galic to his apartment in Hadzici, telling him that he did not need an escort and they were going to his apartment, Dunjic's apartment, for a drink. Once they, Dunjic and Galic, arrived at his apartment, they were joined by Brne's men and after a while persons present came to provoke General Galic and the general was forced to endure the unpleasantness. So, sir, after -- on this evening after this cocktail party, was there an occasion when you went back to your apartment with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you about that, but after that I would kindly ask for a private session, closed session, if possible for private reasons, primarily for the sake of General Galic, Your Honours, if that would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, why don't we first -- why don't you first tell us what happened at the apartment.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it's not that I invited General Galic to my apartment. We were celebrating in the Srbija Hotel in Ilidza and Mr. Morillon was present, the commander of the Foreign Legion, and that unit of the UN. Mr. Galic was present, I was present, and presidents of municipalities were there. There was this official protocol involved. Mr. Galic spoke, Mr. Prstojevic spoke, Mr. Morillon spoke, and I did too. There were cocktails. After the official part, I left that party, and I went to my apartment, and Galic came to my apartment at his own initiative, and privately. He [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] did not come to the command post. He came to my apartment. Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] this --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've asked kindly --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This document written a few days after this event discusses some actions that took place there and it uses the word "unpleasantness," and so should we assume from the event that took place on that evening that your dismissal soon followed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a small imprecision in the transcript. Line 24, [In English] "I did not come to the command post." [Interpretation] The witness said that "he" did not come to the command post. He said that he, the general, did not come to the command post. So if that matters, then it should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer my question. Did you shortly thereafter leave the SRK?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I left shortly afterwards. I was replaced in writing. I received an order, and I obeyed that order.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This document goes on, and it says: "As soon as the military police found out Galic's whereabouts, his escort immediately went there to get him, at which time the clash between him and Brne's Chetniks occurred and also fire was opened from sidearms. From Hadzici General Galic was transferred from Butile and subsequently on to Pale." And then in the last paragraph: "We have been informed in the army circles across the area of Hadzici, Ilidza, and Butile there are rumours that the general was arrested on that occasion and the reason being cited for this is that he had dismissed Major Dunjic from the SRK." Sir, the decision to arrest General Galic, failed decision to arrest General Galic, on that evening, that was a decision that you made all your own just like the arrest you made in December; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: After --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I explain why it's not correct? First of all, you said Mladic and it's not Mladic, it's Galic, and then also there was no decision and General Galic was not arrested, and after that there was no clash with the military police. This entire document is incorrect, because it's not correct that Brne's Chetniks were there. That's not correct either. I was in my apartment as a private person. Commander Galic came with his own escort, armed, into my apartment, and there were a few people there. One was a member of the Ilidza MUP, and then later on the chief of the Ilidza MUP came as well. There were no Chetniks there as you put it, Brne's Chetniks. That is the way you are putting it. Let me be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6006, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness once stated that he wanted to go into private session, but the Chamber saw no reason, so I don't think we need to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We can deal with that in redirect if Dr. Karadzic thinks it's something that should be brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you just mentioned a short time ago that you left shortly thereafter. How quickly did you leave the area?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that was two days after the order, so two days later I left on my own for Serbia. I believe it was two days later. I can't tell you with great precision, perhaps a day or two or three, but I left the command post immediately and then privately I returned and went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And even after you left, isn't it true that Brne and his unit went on to live up to his criminal reputation? You knew about that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Once I received the order, I was absolutely not interested in any of that. Once I received the order to leave the post of brigade commander, I had no further interest in that, absolutely nothing, after I left that area. This would have been the 26th or the 27th of January, so I didn't care anymore about the unit or anything else, because I was disappointed. I was disappointed by this decision and the actions that led to this incident. This is why I requested a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Who took over the command of the brigade after you left?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe a few days after I left Mr. Spasoje Cojic arrived but I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P02305.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is something that happened a couple weeks later. I'd like to see if you know about it. This is another MUP document, and it regards that gentleman. We're just going to read the first paragraph. It's February 12th, official note: "We are in possession of intelligence that paramilitary formations, more specifically the group commanded by Branislav Gavrilovic, aka Brne, knew the exact date of the arrival of the new commander of the Igman Brigade and were even preparing his liquidation. Namely, the mentioned group of Chetniks, while the brigade was commanded by Major ... Dunjic, had the freedom of decision and practically implemented some of their own ideas, both in the political sphere and in military life." Sir, up until that point, and this is February of 1993, would you agree that Brne's unit under the power of the local civilian political authorities and the republican level political authorities operated outside the command of the SRK and under your command, which is the reason you were dismissed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you're confusing me. Yesterday, you suggested that Mr. Gavrilovic had problems with Prstojevic, whereas now you're suggesting that he was under their command. So all of this is absolutely unclear to me. And as for this document, I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the reference which would suggest that Brne was under the command of the republican leadership, under their influence? Fifteen, 16, 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This regards evidence that you received in Prosecution case in chief. An example of that would be the intercept we showed yesterday between Brne Gavrilovic and Seselj where Seselj indicated that he had just spoken to -- he had called Karadzic's office and left a message that he was going to take all the paramilitaries out if Karadzic didn't do something about it. You also received evidence that -- you've also received evidence that other members of the republican political leadership, for example, Plavsic have had involvement with the paramilitaries and that's the basis of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I just want to briefly go back to something that you talked about yesterday, and you spoke about this a few times, and you said that ideological differences somehow influenced whether people understood units to be paramilitary or not. And at transcript 30506, you said: [As read] "I'm telling you that paramilitary units in the heads of many officers of the former JNA were paramilitary only because they were called Vucak, Wolves, and other names, and by the same analogy the Deltas and the seals are also paramilitary formations. Those how those people reasoned due to ideological differences, whereas I was not interested in any ideological differences." So I just want to touch upon this briefly because it still remains a little bit unclear to me. Is it your testimony that someone who had a more objective perspective, someone who was not burdened by ideological differences may not consider, for example, Brne's unit to then paramilitaries? Do I understand this correctly?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have P02855, please. So I want to take your example and then show you a document and ask you a question about this. And in particular you mentioned the Wolves. We're going to look at a document from July of 1992, and it's a report on paramilitary formations in the territory. And this is a report from Tolimir at the time. And in the first paragraph he writes: [As read] "Paramilitary formations and groups are an important feature of the war in the former Yugoslavia. The paramilitary formations in the territory have special identifying names." And he lists the names. And one of the names he lists are the Wolves, which is something you mentioned. And they display iconography ranging from Orthodox ornaments and symbols to Chetnik and Vietnam war symbols. And then he goes on and says: "Their main characteristics are as follows: They're mostly composed of individuals of low moral quality and in many cases of persons previously prosecuted for crimes and offences and even convicted for crimes of murder, robbery, larceny, and the like. And very often such units have in their rank pathological criminals whom the conditions of war and general lawlessness have brought to the fore." And if we can turn to page 4 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S, please. It's towards the bottom in the English and it's going to be at the top of the B/C/S. It speaks about the Wolves detachment: "The detachment of Veljko Milankovic from Prnjavor has about 150 men and is, as of recently, formally under the command of the 1st KK. Members of this detachment are involved in extensive looting and recently attacked the Tactical Group 3 command post, arresting one SR BH army colonel in the process." So now we've taken your example, the Wolves. Would you agree with me from what we've read, and maybe perhaps from what you might have known, would you agree in this case even an objective observer might consider this behaviour that I've described to be a negative influence?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, 20 years after the war, this statement -- or, rather, this document will provoke a reaction among the people from where the Wolves are. They will provoke laughter first and then disappointment. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was a fighter for the Serb matter for the survival of the Serb people in this area and his unit, irrespective of this document, cannot be classified as a paramilitary unit, and you can check that now 20 years after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you for your comments. I just want to address one last topic with you, and it's something that you yourself has brought to your attention and today you did it for the fourth time. You -- you mentioned a Republika Srpska Supreme Court decision of 1992, and as I understand it, you're suggesting that it's -- this decision gave you a reason or gave you some sort of rationale as to why you legitimately took Brne's group under your command and they weren't paramilitaries anymore. They didn't qualify as paramilitaries anymore. Can you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I did not care about ideological differences. The unit, or, rather, the Savo Derikonja Detachment, was already there within the area of responsibility of the brigade when I arrived. I abided by the decision of the Supreme Court. And this unit, as I've already said in my statement, had not committed any crime that would be a breach that would constitute a breach of the Geneva Conventions, and you also saw and I told you a moment ago what the percentage of men in that unit was. You could see that I did not pay much attention to this unit, not because I wanted to cover anything up, but because our focus was totally elsewhere and not on what you've been insisting on for the past two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, the concept of the Supreme Court decision giving you some cover was not at all mentioned in your statement, yet you have four times brought it up during your testimony. Was this decision discussed for the first time during your proofing with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't even discuss this either with the Defence team or Mr. Karadzic, the decision of the Supreme Court. And as I've already told you, it wasn't just a decision that guided me but also my ideological beliefs. I didn't care where a fighter came from or what their past was. All I saw was a fighter who would obey my orders, and I didn't care about what their future would be or what their past was. I was focused as a professional soldier only on the defence of some 10.000 or so Serb people there, whereas who was a member of the Radical Party or the Communist Party or the SDS, I couldn't care less. Whether someone had been -- had served a prison term before they arrived there, that was irrelevant to me. All that I cared about was that they would obey my orders. And again, I have to repeat that they constituted 1 to 3 per cent of the total number of men in my unit. So not only was I not interested in this or involved in thinking about this, that was not the primary concern of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I noticed yesterday and again today that you have some written notes in front of you that you refer to. Are those your own handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are my own notes, handwritten notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I see that they're on the back side of the actual statement. Were these notes taken recently during your proofing or are these notes from some other time?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, this is not a statement, but I did also jot something down on the statement itself, but the documents that I received jogged my memory, so then I just jotted some things down, and I don't see that there's any problem with that. As a responsible person, I felt that I needed to prepare for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Nor do I. I was just enquiring about the notes. Can we have 65 ter 17403. Sir, I want to show you one more document. 17403, please. And I suspect you probably haven't seen this before. This is the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska, and we're going to focus in on numbers 743 and 744, and in the English, that would be page 3, please. And for 744, this speaks about a decision that took place in the Assembly on August 12th, 1992. This is about -- less than a month before you came. And the Assembly adopted the following decision on the establishment of the Supreme Court of the Republika Srpska, that the Supreme Court Republika Srpska is being established, and then the next cite, 744, says the Assembly during the session held on November 24, 1992 - so this is well after you came - adopted the following decision on the appointment of the judge of the Supreme Court of the Republika Srpska and then it gives the name. Mr. Dunjic, it's difficult to see how the Supreme Court's first decision could have been in effect giving you leeway to adopt paramilitaries into your brigade in September of 1992 when the judges had not yet fully been appointed by November of 1992. Can you understand how this doesn't make any sense?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do you think it's misleading? What's your basis, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because the judges were changing all the time. I mean, one judge would be appointed, another one would have left. And it doesn't show here that the -- that this was a complete panel of judges. It was just the appointment of this one particular judge.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last portion of his reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last sentence, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the suit was established, there were already Chambers that could operate, that could work, and there were two levels of court. They could work at two levels. But the judges kept changing. There were new judges being appointed, other ones -- the old ones would have left, and so on. And it doesn't say anywhere here that the court was in fact established in November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness has heard already what Mr. Karadzic said, but would you like to respond, Ms. West, or reformulate your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think at this point maybe we'll show him another document and then we can go from there. P01468, please. And these are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: These are minutes from an Assembly session end of October, early November 1992. And if we can go to page 2 of the English we're looking at the agenda and it's number 31. And on the agenda at this date there is a draft decision on appointment of the Republika Srpska Supreme Court judges. So Mr. Dunjic you've -- you've seen these documents. You've heard my question. You've heard even Mr. Karadzic's comments, but can you tell us how it is in -- on September 4th 1992, when you entered -- appointed brigade commander, a Supreme Court decision already existed somehow making paramilitaries legal and legitimate members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously you either did not read my statement properly or perhaps you did it deliberately, but I state there that soon, and I didn't say on the 4th of September, I said that soon that unit was placed under the command, under my command. And I said yesterday that in the second half of 1992, there was a decision that provided for these units being treated not as paramilitary. They wouldn't have that attribute. But, rather, as volunteer units. And I didn't mention the 4th of September, nor did I say that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you tender that Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you for that reminder. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We object, Mr. President. There's no basis for it. The witness hasn't provided any basis for the point upon which Ms. West sought to make; in fact, there is to problem with the Official Gazette in principle, but there's no relevance given the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the fact that a judge was appointed and the -- after the -- following the establishment of the Supreme Court not relevant, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's not relevant. For example, the de jure appointment doesn't mean that the ICTY came into existence that day. So it's not relevant to anything. The appointment of a single judge is not relevant to any point that was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Only to say, Your Honour, that that was not the only thing that was pointed out in the gazette. The other matter had to do with the decision on the establishment of the Supreme Court itself which happened less than a month before this gentleman came into command. So I would imagine that's -- that's relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to warn that in this document, too, you could see that people were relieved of duty and new people appointed. This was an ongoing process. You can see it if you look at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what probative value it will have is a matter to be assessed later on, but the Chamber finds it relevant at the moment, prima facie, and we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6007, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I take it you have something to -- for your re-examination. Do you think you can finish it in relatively short period of time? Otherwise, we'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellency. I can be even quicker, because I don't have any redirect other than I would like to thank Mr. Dunjic, but I would also like to point something out that has nothing to do with the witness himself but has to do with the way -- the questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there are matters to be asked by my colleagues, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Dunjic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who is the next witness, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mile Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it given the time --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say one sentence if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the words of the Defence or the Prosecutor do not constitute evidence, but I would really appreciate it if Ms. West quoted documents properly. For instance, the 5528 document -- or, rather, P2228, there is no mention of paramilitaries, but, rather, volunteers, and there is also no mention that he called the foreign office but, rather, Pale, and that he couldn't reach Radovan. This would help to avoid misleading the witness. Because this is what Madam West said on page 27: "Thank you, Mr. President. This regards evidence that you received in Prosecution in chief. An example would be an intercept you saw yesterday between Brne Gavrilovic and Seselj, where Seselj said he called Karadzic's office and said he was going to take all paramilitaries out if Karadzic didn't do something about it." [Interpretation] So the interpretation that was given to this intercept is completely false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was a submission made in response to Chamber's request, but -- but your point has been made, and we note it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll redact the lines 21 to 22 of page 3. The Chamber will have a break for half an hour and resume at 5 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning. Could the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D6400 in e-court. We have it in Serbian, too, although this is sufficient. Mr. Sladoje will probably be able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, did you provide a statement to the Defence team and is it the statement that is before you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for interpretation, and I would kindly ask you to do the same since we speak the same language, and we don't want to create problems for the interpreters. Does this statement contain accurately what you stated?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions here today as the ones that were put to you during the taking of the statement, would your answers be basically the same?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now read out the summary in the English language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is admitted. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. Just before any ruling on the admission of the statement, I'd have one request. The redaction, and I've spoken to my friend Mr. Robinson about this, the redaction of paragraph 28 of the statement which relates to a dropped incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to raise that issue, but both parties agree to that redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll agree to that redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then -- otherwise no objection to the admission of the statement as well as four associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have one point with respect to one associated exhibit, but there's no problem in admitting them at this moment. Shall we give the number now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Statement 65 ter 1D6400 will be Exhibit D2479; 65 ter number 1D8556 will be D2480; 65 ter 1D8557 will be Exhibit D2481; 65 ter number 1D8558 will be Exhibit D2482, and 65 ter number 1D8559 will be Exhibit D2483.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Mile Sladoje is an economist by education and training. He completed his compulsory military service in Kragujevac and Ruma in 1973 and 1974 in the artillery branch. He first learned about the arming of Muslim forces in 1991, when a Muslim business associate asked him if he was interested in selling ammunition, offer which he declined. He was a member of the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade. From April 1992 until June 1992, he was commander of the Nedzarici Barracks. From June 1992 until March 1993, he was assistant commander of the battalion for moral and religious affairs. From March 1993 until October 1993, he was battalion commander, and then when three battalions merged into one, he was appointed assistant commander for logistics and half a year later assistant commander for the newly formed battalion. His battalion did not have a single professional officer nor trained snipers. Following March 1992, local Serbs held neighbourhood watches in front of their houses. After successfully repelling an attack by Muslim paramilitaries on 8th of April, 1992, local Serbs continued to organise themselves and eventually formed a line of defence, which remained more or less unchanged until the end of the war. The opposing units belonged to the 101st and 102nd Brigade of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. His battalion was in an inferior position since buildings in the area under Muslim control were mostly high-rises from where they fired with snipers. Muslim forces also blocked access to their positions with mines. Their front lines were only 30 to 50 metres away from his unit's position. All positions held by the opposing brigades were in civilian areas. There was not a single entire -- entirely civilian settlement there in which they did not have an enemy unit or a military target. His unit also had knowledge of the existence of enemy military targets in the depth of the enemy territory. The orders of the brigade were to use ammunition sparingly and only when attacked by the enemy. His battalion conducted exclusively defensive operation -- operations except for a single occasion when they improved their tactical position on Stupsko Brdo to facilitate defence. The goal of his battalion was to defend their houses, protect the civilian population, and prevent Muslim forces from reaching Ilidza. Had the opposing forces broken out in the parts of Sarajevo under Muslim control -- under Serbian control, it would have had a critical impact on the other fronts on the -- in the course of the war in BH. The permanent order for his battalion was to open fire only in response to enemy fire and only at observed firing positions. It is possible that there were civilian collateral casualties on the line of disengagement since their firing positions were in the vicinity or in apartment buildings themselves. He had no intention of causing civilian casualties or terrorising or exerting psychological pressure on civilians under the control of Muslim authorities and has never heard anyone in his unit, the superior commands or civilian authorities had such intentions. His unit never received or issued any such order, orally or written. On the contrary, superior commands and him personally issued orders that civilians in the part of the city under Muslim control should not be the target of an attack. Conversely, civilians in his zone of responsibility, including women, were often targeted by snipers or subjected to the artillery attack. His unit built makeshift sniper barriers from the blankets, tarpaulins, wooden planks and plywood which blocked the view of the enemy snipers. His brigade complained to UNPROFOR about frequent enemy attacks from civilian zones. When fired -- when fire was returned, they would complain that his unit was targeting civilian facilities. The brigade did not prevent the delivery of humanitarian aid, except when they had information that they were bringing -- were being used for illegitimate purposes as was in case in 1994 when flack jackets were confiscated from the French battalion convoy. Soon afterwards the rapid intervention forces targeted Serbian positions with particular intensity on civilian buildings, causing several civilian casualties. They had knowledge that goods from humanitarian aid convoys had passed through their zone of responsibility and were being sold in the black market and exorbitant -- exorbitant prices and the Serb civilians had to pay to be able to flee from -- to Serb-held territory. Regarding incidents at Hakije Turajlic 33 [sic] in Dobrinja on 12th of July, 1993, Mile Sladoje states that no orders to target civilians were issued and that no line of sight existed between their positions and the scene of the alleged incident. Regarding incident in the area of Alipasino Polje on 22nd of January, 1994, Mile Sladoje states that there were no mortars at Home for the Blind and that no one from their command ordered the shelling of the place of the alleged incident. Regarding the incident of 18 June 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wouldn't normally interrupt Dr. Karadzic at this point, but we've just agreed to redact that evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. This one is redacted, yes? Okay. Regarding the incident near the junction of Nikole Demonje at Bulevar Avnoja in Dobrinja on 25th of May, 1994, Mile Sladoje states that no orders to fire at that intersection were issued, that no line of sight existed between their positions and the scene of the alleged incident and that they did not have snipers with that kind of range in their battalion. Regarding incident at Djure Jaksica Street in the west end of Sarajevo on the 26th of June, 1994, Mile Sladoje states that no orders were issued to fire at the girl who was allegedly killed at the scene of this incident. [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no questions for Mr. Sladoje at this point in time. I turn the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, shall we upload 1D8558. Which is entitled as "Military positions of ABiH in civilian zones." In para 18, the witness stated that a police station, RTV building, wire factory, the UNPROFOR base, Astra and Uniklima, all these buildings were marked, but I wonder whether the UNPROFOR base was also marked on this map. Mr. Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The PTT in Djering [phoen] building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So UNPROFOR was based on that building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As you noted, Mr. Sladoje, your evidence in chief was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you'll be cross-examined by the Prosecution. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, we've already met one another yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And thank you for that. I'd like to start your cross-examination by asking you to confirm a few of the things we discussed, if that's okay. So first of all, can you confirm you were actually based in Nedzarici area throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your battalion headquarters was initially located at the barracks and in the barracks compound in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And at the end of 1993, when the first 1st, 2nd and 3rd Battalions of the Ilidza Brigade which covered Nedzarici, Aerodromsko Nasilje, and Kasindol were amalgamated into one battalion, this headquarters was moved to a location on Kasindolska Street.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In March 1993, you succeeded Radivoje Grkovic as commander of the Serb portions in Nedzarici when he left the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you were eventually replaced by Svetozar Guzina, who took the post of battalion commander when the three battalions were joined into one?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And yesterday, you agreed with the estimate that the Nedzarici Barracks compound was about 300 to 350 metres from the school for the blind; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the Faculty of Theology -- as for the Faculty of Theology which you mentioned in your statement, would you agree with the estimate that it's about 200 metres from the barracks compound?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Between 150 and 200.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And yesterday I showed you a map that you saw was a black and white version of your own marked map which is now D2481, but that had been extended to show the approach to the airport, and I asked you to mark your battalion's entire area of responsibility on that map. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at 65 ter 24222.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I hope shortly on the screen you'll be able to see the map you marked yesterday. Now, we see -- well, first of all, do you recognise the map that you marked yesterday on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the -- do the green lines on this map extend -- or more accurately, do they represent the complete area of responsibility of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the green dot on this map with the letters KP on it, do you agree that the green dot denotes the location of the check-point on Kasindolska Street?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that check-point is on the road that the UN used to and from the airport; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that check-point was under your battalion's control?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It was not under our control, because one could freely pass through.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who operated that check-point?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No one did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour. I realised that I've completely forgotten, in fact, it's not necessarily for the Prosecution to request that, but I've forgotten to request that the witness be given a caution pursuant to Rule 90, and those sorts of matters, obviously better late than never. So if I could just pause and extend my apologies for having forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Mr. Sladoje, although you have already started giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. I mean by "incriminate," I meant something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sladoje. Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, and apologies again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we'll move on from that last point, Mr. Sladoje, to just conclude this brief section related to our discussion yesterday. Can you confirm that yesterday you also indicated you were linked with the Ilidza Brigade command by way of an induction communication system?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also had means -- you were also able to communicate with the brigade command by telephone?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would use couriers during combat activities in the event other means of communication were inoperative?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The Ilidza Brigade command was headquartered on the Velika Aleja in Ilidza in the former Sipad building?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And battalion commanders briefed the Ilidza Brigade commander every day by telephone?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And battalion commanders also attended briefing meetings at the brigade headquarters, but those were held no more than once a week at best and also depending on the need.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that concludes the areas we discussed yesterday. I'd like to move on to some specific parts of your statement and refer to paragraph 6 to begin with where you mention two areas, Vojnicko Polje and Mojmilo. And in that regard I'd like to show you a photograph. It's a panoramic photograph, 65 ter number 24212. Do you see a photograph on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if my colleague would be able to just zoom in one magnification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sladoje, this picture was taken in August 1996 from scaffolding at the theological faculty, and I'm just wondering if you could tell us do you see these two areas you referred to in paragraph 6, Mojmilo and Vojnicko Polje? And if you need to have this zoomed in a bit more, just say.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes. Mojmilo is to the right and Vojnicko Polje to the left. There is more to those areas than we can see here, but there they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could my colleague then zoom in on the hill in the centre of this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I invite you, Mr. Sladoje, to take the marker in front of you and draw a circle around the area you recognise as Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you mark that with an M?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Vojnicko Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, that's marked with a VP.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have you put your initials on this zoomed-in image and date that, please. It's the 28th of November today.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could that be a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6008, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
