utterances.text: Do you want to tender the previous map marked by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour, and apologies. I had completely forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted as Exhibit P6009.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could we go back to the underlined panorama, 65 ter 24212, and zoom a little bit to the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sladoje, would you agree that to the right of the area you marked as being Mojmilo you see part of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are those the apartment buildings in the distance?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just mark Dobrinja, as you've done before, with a circle.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks] I made a mistake. It looks like D6, whereas it should be D5, because that's the name of the settlement, Dobrinja 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can delete it and rewrite.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what's the apartment blocks that you see even further to the right of Dobrinja 5?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: That is also Dobrinja, Dobrinja 1, Dobrinja 2, and Dobrinja 3 and 4 would be further afield, but we can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the apartment blocks to your right you recognise as the areas of Dobrinja 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just mark those the same way, please, with a D1 and a D2.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks] One cannot see Dobrinja 2 in the photograph. The buildings here are in Dobrinja 1, whereas Dobrinja 2 and its buildings are behind that. It's not easy to mark it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. Could we get you to sign and date this image, please, and we'll do one more marking on this panorama before we leave it.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could that be the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6010, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go back to the unlined panorama, please, 24212. And if we could go over to the left-hand side of the image now, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, is that the area -- is that part of the area of Alipasino Polje that you see to the left-hand side of the panorama, Mr. Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you mark that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just sign and date, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just on this panorama, that would be the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours, and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6011, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you not think that we need to admit the whole panorama as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Reid was asking me that very question, Your Honour, and I wasn't sure yet, but now that we've come to the end, I think it's quite appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit P6012.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sladoje, based on the information in your statement, would you agree that these are some of the civilian areas where people lived in apartment buildings that you've described?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, civilians did live there. These are civilian neighbourhoods, but between Nedzarici and these buildings there was a line of separation and fighting took place there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And based on the evidence in your statement, you would agree that these areas Vojnicko Polje, Mojmilo, Dobrinja, Alipasino Polje are all areas that you could reach with your weapons? They were in range of your weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And also in your statement you said there was not a single entirely civilian settlement there which didn't have an enemy unit or other military target in it. So from that, could we say that there's actually no area that you saw on this panorama where you didn't expect civilians to be?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: That's not what I stated. There were civilians there, but among the civilians it was the military that was using practically all buildings for their purposes. Say in Mojmilo it was the sports hall that was used for putting up units. Elementary schools, kindergartens and other big buildings were used for these purposes. Most often that's what they did. They located their units among the civilian population and it is impossible to say practically for any area that there were no units -- there were no civilians there. People had to live somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 of your statement you said the permanent order for your battalion was "to open fire only in response to enemy fire and only at observed firing positions." So I want to ask you to explain what that means. Does that mean it's okay to shoot provided you were only responding to enemy fire from positions you saw firing?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Well, you explained it very well. I wouldn't have anything special to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And was there a requirement that your response -- no. I'll move on, actually. Now, if we go over to paragraph 18 and the map you marked as D2482, you named a number of what you considered to be military targets, and I'd like to look at D2482, which was 65 ter number 1D8558. Can you see that clearly, Mr. Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, now, were able to -- you marked the Standard factory, the Zora chocolate factory, and the TAM factory. Were you able to see those locations from your positions?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that these were -- these locations were actually front-line locations? They aren't in depth at all, are they?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No. They were in depth of the territory in terms of the separation line. They were further away.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How far?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Well, the Standard would be, say, 1 kilometre, perhaps somewhat less. I'm not quite sure. If we'd start with the Standard building, then we could go on the same number of kilometres. The student dormitories, the wire factory is a bit further off. I marked those locations because that's where soldiers were involved in preparations. That's where they were receiving ammunition. They used this for their normal purposes, and they also had machinery in these factories. I was familiar with these factories. So they used this for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And these places, some of which you've just mentioned and some of which you've not, Geodeski, Vodovod, RTV, Astra, Uniklima, RNK, Tornica Zica [phoen], those actually weren't in your direct line of sight, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No. No. We couldn't see Uniklima, Astra, Boras, the land survey institute. They're further away, so we could not see those facilities. However, according to the intelligence we had and according to what we heard from people who were coming from Sarajevo, we knew that these buildings were used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, actually, you couldn't see the UNPROFOR headquarters from your locations either, because we just saw on the panorama that you had the skyscraper apartment buildings of Alipasino Polje in the way.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: They could be seen from the left-hand side of the positions that we held. It wasn't a particularly good view, but you could see the configuration of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you named streets. You named Prvomajska and Geteova Street, and to your knowledge because you're from Sarajevo, those were also residential areas where civilians lived in apartment buildings, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes. But also there were soldiers in each and every neighbourhood. The civilian population lived in Nedzarici. There was the barracks there. There was this unity of the army and the civilian population, because impossible to live in any other way. That is to say that not a single neighbourhood was civilian only. It is a neighbourhood where people live, but also the military was stationed there, and that is practically the way it is in all urban areas where there was a military presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you must accept, given what you've just said, that there's a pretty high risk of civilian casualties when firing on any of these areas in the depth of the city.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Correct, but how can you expect us not to open fire if our positions are jeopardised? And the other side includes both civilians and soldiers. They are both present there. So it is the soldiers who are firing at us that are jeopardising the civilians on that side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene in the transcript. The witness said, "How could we open fire at enemy soldiers who are jeopardising our positions and our soldiers and civilians."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "How could we not open fire."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can we not open fire? How can we not open fire if we are jeopardised. How can we not open fire at enemy soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can carry on. Do you confirm having said that, Mr. Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat it once again. This is what I said: If fire is opened by the enemy side against our positions, it is not possible. Perhaps this would be a clearer answer: It is not possible for us to fire at military objectives only without jeopardising the civilian population because they were there and very often civilians were used for that kind of thing. Even if they were not used for that kind of thing people had to live there and military units operated from such an area, so in fact they were among civilians and that is why this happened, as I stated. There was this collateral damage among the civilians because we fired at military targets. I do not exclude the possibility of civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked in your statement about a couple of incidents, one of them being the shelling of a waterline on 12 July 1993, and you said you heard about this incident a few days after it allegedly happened. I have two questions. First of all, why do you say "allegedly" in your statement? Are you disputing the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I am still not sure that the incident did occur because the Muslim side often took advantage of such gatherings. Even when there was a cease-fire, all of a sudden incidents would occur during those days. My suspicion is that they did this on purpose in order to accuse us and I heard about that in incident on television. It was possible to watch BH television. I found out about that, and later on I did not investigate the matter and also I did not have an opportunity of seeing any kind of ballistic findings, but my suspicion is that these shells were fired from Butmir. There was a factory there Hidrogradnja, or, rather, Sigma. And most often that's where they operated from because that is across Nedzarici and most often it was the people and commander of Nedzarici who were accused because this was coming from that side and what is symptomatic is that they would have people gather to play ball in such areas; for example, a little girl playing in an area where there were operations. This is simply something that is staged, rigged, incorrect therefore.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said it was possible to watch BiH TV. So what did you hear about this incident on BiH TV?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Well, I just heard that it happened. It was those brief news and nothing more than that. Also, the accusation that this had been fired from the positions in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just about your positions. In respect of this incident, you also said that no line of sight -- there was no line of sight between your positions and the scene of the incident, but you have some experience now, after your training with the JNA and your service, some experience with mortars, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, do you know that -- you must know that a mortar is an indirect fire weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. May I just ask you something, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you have a question, Mr. Sladoje, I think it's more appropriate that you direct your questions to the Chamber rather than to me.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I do apologise. I didn't know what the rules were. Mr. President, may I put a question to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. You're not supposed to ask a question, but in the course of your response if there's anything you'd like to add, you may do so, Mr. Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just agreed that a mortar is an indirect fire --

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting. I didn't mean to. You just agreed that a mortar is an indirect fire weapon so you must also know that mortar crews don't actually need a line of sight to acquire and engage a target.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. I know that. However, there is this other thing. When I said that we did not have a line of sight, that meant that at that point in time when there was a gathering taking place somewhere, we had no idea that people were gathering there. We could not see that. We did not know that. So that's why I'm saying it. That's why I'm putting it that way. I mean, it would be a layman's -- a layman's statement if I were to say that a mortar can open direct fire only. Of course I know how a mortar fires. So that is where the difference is. I believe that you were in Nedzarici and in Dobrinja, and it's probably clear to you what the positions are, where we were and where the other side was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to move on to another one of those incidents, and it's a sniping incident. You talked about it in your statement, and it involves an allegation of firing - and I'll give you exactly the paragraph number - firing at an intersection on Bulevar Avnoja and Nikole Demonje Streets in Dobrinja, and you said that the distance between the target at that intersection and the theological faculty was over 1.500 metres away. So I'd like to ask you since you know the distance between the target and the faculty, do you have any idea of the distance between the target and the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Well, I knew that earlier on because I lived in that area and I knew how far away Dobrinja was, and that's why I stated that. This incident if it occurred about 1.500 metres away, we did not have a sniper rifle with that kind of range. The range of a sniper rifle is usually between 800 metres and 1.200 metres. And I know that you assumed that it was fired from the Faculty of Theology. We did not have a sniper there. There is that opening there, and it was claimed that that was a sniper nest. We did have a recoilless gun there, and we used it in contravention of military rules because we had no other way of dealing with the guns at Alipasino Polje. We could only do it by using a recoilless gun.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some more questions, Mr. Sladoje, and when you do that you might have to lean forward a little bit more so the interpreters can hear your answers more clearly. This Chamber has actually received evidence Mr. Sladoje that the gap between the incident location and the confrontation line is approximately 550 metres. And for the record that's in P1620, page 54. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could agree as far as the front of our defence position is concerned, because there is one position at Dobrinja 5, and then there's also Dobrinja 2 and 3 there. And from these positions one could not operate at all because if you noticed these buildings in Dobrinja 5, there is this entire line there. There is the line of separation there, so you cannot really operate in that way from these positions where these positions are 550 metres away. Now, if what you mean is the Faculty of Theology, that is further afield. Now, I don't know which positions you're referring to. From which position did you think that this could be engaged?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Well, I think I was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I was pretty clear. My question was about the distance between the incident and the confrontation line, and I understand you to agree that it was approximately 550 metres between the incident site and your forward defence positions.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I agree, but I do not agree with another thing you said. You insist that we fired from the point where the distance between our sides was the smallest. I don't see how you can claim that, that it came from the forward line or that it came from Stupsko Brdo. I mean, there was also the Stupsko Brdo where we had positions by the institute for the blind. That is where we differ. I explained that, and could you please check this once again. Our closest separation line with Dobrinja 5 was 100 to 150 metres perhaps even not that much. However, this Dobrinja 5 sheltered Dobrinja 2 and Dobrinja 3. We could not operate there if --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, we're getting a little bit off topic, and I'm going to try and bring you back to the topic by calling up something for you to look at. It's P1620, page 54, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that we will not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, can you explain why this should be confidential?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually have no idea, Your Honours. I was completely surprised to hear that it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that certain part of this document is confidential, and we have a public redacted version as P1621. Shall we use that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again my apologies. I'm doing that a lot this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now that we have this, can we just enlarge the photo on the top of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sladoje, the blue circle on this photo, which is the top photo on page -- on P1621, page 54, the blue circle marks the location of the incident. The arrow where you see the box that says "550 metres" is the approximate location of the confrontation lines. Can you just answer yes or no, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I cannot discern or recognise this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a satellite image that marks the location of the incident in green, anti-sniping barriers, that marks the location of the confrontation lines at 550 metres from the incident location. Would you agree that 550 metres is an accurate estimate of the location of the confrontation lines from the incident location?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I'm saying once again I'm not familiar with this image. Can you please explain it a bit to me. Where does this red marking start? Where is this actually from? I mean, please help me with this. Help me identify this position here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll move on and I'll come back to it in a different way. Thank you. I want to come back to the subject of humanitarian aid. In your statement at paragraph 23, you said that in the fall of 1994, you stopped a convoy of French battalion at the intersection of Kasindolska Street - that's the check-point that you said nobody ran - and confiscated 90 flack jackets intended for Muslim forces. So under whose orders did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: We found out by way of intelligence that the French, the French battalion, were transporting flack jackets, and this was not humanitarian aid. We received this intelligence from the brigade command because that is at brigade level, and at the intersection at the check-point we stopped the French soldiers and we found 90 flack jackets. On the basis of my statement, you said now that it had been unmanned. Well, it wasn't manned all the time, but it was from time to time. There wasn't any need for someone to be there all the time because our positions were nearby and all humanitarian convoys went by normally unless in such situations when we received this kind of information beforehand. It is a fact we took away flack jackets. I think you would agree with that, that flack jackets are not humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you received this information from the brigade command, nobody told you that the flack jackets were actually the property of the UNPROFOR French battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: They were the property of the French battalion, but the French battalion was deployed at the airport. It didn't have a unit of its own in Sarajevo. So there was no need for it to transport these flack jackets. I don't believe that soldiers from another country would transport flack jackets to another army, because each army has their own logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what did you do with the flack jackets? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: We handed them over to the brigade command, and of course they were later used by the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Later used by the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So they were never returned to the UN forces?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P2455. It's a document that's unfortunately only in English, so I'm going to read you a passage that I'd like to ask you about. It's an UNPROFOR Weekly Situation Report for the week of 5 to 11 March 1995. And if we could go over to page 5, paragraph 12, there's something I want to ask you about. This says that on March 9 1995 - and it's about a halfway through the paragraph - the Serbs stopped a French truck with 126 new advanced flak jackets valued at 350.000 Deutschmarks and the Serbs took the truck and the flak jackets but allowed the soldiers to go free. So reading this, it actually sounds like there was more than one instance where you confiscated flak jackets. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of my battalion, or, rather, the 1st Battalion command there was only one such instance. Perhaps this happened elsewhere, but I'm not aware of that case, that incident. But I declare with full responsibility that this happened only once, as I've said. Whether the figure was correct I'm not absolutely certain, but it did happen as I related it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So perhaps we're talking about the same incident because earlier in this paragraph the author writes: "At the infamous Sierra 4, an illegal Serb check-point on the main road from the city to the airport, another hijacking has taken place." So could we be talking about the same incident?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It is possible. Sierra 4 is precisely the check-point that I indicated, that I marked, but I repeat, I only know of one incident and I was present when it happened. Now, whether this was elsewhere or whether there was a difference in the number of these flak jackets, I really don't know, because I have no reason to deny it, nor am I trying to do so because I know that there was a report of -- by the UNPROFOR. There was also a report compiled, and there is no reason for me to deny this. I never even tried to do so, because that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, let's look at another document, 65 ter number 90240. It's - again in English, unfortunately - an UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo Weekly Situation Report for 7 April 1995, and at page 2 of this document it -- under the heading "Problems at Sierra 4, city blockaded," it has something I'd like to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Page 2. Oh, and the document's only got one page uploaded, so I think we'll probably just move on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually have only one last question to ask you about, and it's about paragraph 25 of your statement where you talk about the Fatima Gunic school, and you said that, "If the former name of the school is the Andrija Raso school ..." You had some information from a cousin who said that the school was used to house soldiers. So my question to you is: Assuming this school was previously the Andrija Raso school and it did at some point house soldiers, to your knowledge was it fired on by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Well, first, I would like to correct something. I didn't say that my cousin provided this information. I received that information from other sources. Now, she lived in Mojmilo, and she worked at the school Andrija Raso, and she left Mojmilo in 1992, in May, and based on intelligence, that's where we got information that there was -- there were soldiers deployed at the school, and at the point where we were absolutely certain that there were soldiers deployed at a school, that's the only time that we would open fire. Otherwise, absolutely not, because the school would be for children and that would have been against all rules and international laws.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to intervene here. The witness also said, and it didn't make it into the transcript, that there were soldiers in other schools too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. When I mentioned all schools, I mean where we were, at the area where we were, Alipasino Polje and so on. So that is -- those are the schools that I'm referring to. I don't know what happened elsewhere in the centre or Novi Grad areas. I wouldn't know about that. I was not really interested because we weren't anywhere near there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you know that the Andrija Raso school was renamed the Mesa Selimovic school in November 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I didn't know that. And what I said was if that was the school that I meant -- now, I know where Andrija Raso school was, but in view of the fact that almost all street names have changed in Sarajevo, every square and everything, I really wouldn't know what new names would be. I'm not really a tourist guide.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you know who Fatima Gunic was?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Fatima Gunic was a teacher, and she was killed in a shelling on 9 November 1993, in a makeshift classroom. Had you heard anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: She was giving lessons at the time, and a shell fell in front of or outside of the barricaded makeshift classroom, and some children were also killed and there was an investigation. Had you heard about that investigation? You watched the media?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No. No. I really haven't, not really, nor do I know that that happened, nor do I know who this Gunic person was. I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you know that -- so then you heard no information to the effect that the shell was actually found by local investigators to have been fired from Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I've never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Your indulgence for just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, your Excellency. I would just like to thank the witness, but I have no question for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Sladoje. I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go, and we will rise all together. We will have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 10 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.21 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I request a Rule 90(E) warning, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question, but in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we begin, could we please have the term "discretion to oblige you" to be interpreted to the witness as something that is binding rather than a measure of coercion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I take it Mr. Kovacevic has understood it. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Should I address you by rank since you have been trained at our military academy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are still in our armed forces, although it has been significantly reduced.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm warrant officer first class these days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please 1D6401 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're on that topic, the highest rank in the army nowadays is that of brigadier; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you provide a statement to my Defence team, Mr. Kovacevic, and can you see it in the English language before you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it contain what you have stated? In other words, is it accurate? Was it read back to you, and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If today in this courtroom I were to put the same questions, would your answers be basically the same?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, to the fourth document -- fifth document, 1D08458, on the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Which is dealt with in para 20, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's concerning 1997, and I just don't see the relevance to the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Following the Dayton Accords, all officials in Bosnia and Herzegovina had to undergo strict background checks by the OACD and the High Representative when they were allowed to continue working in any public institution, including the armed forces. Only those who had not committed mistakes in the past have been allowed back, in other words, who had a clean slate to start. This is very important from the point of view of credibility as well as conduct during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive it. After reading out the summary, I would like you to deal with the previous one, 1D8457, with the witness directly, because it's not clear from the statement what this item relates to, if you wish to tender that. Please continue -- we'll admit the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2484, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we will admit the first four items first. Shall we give -- but the first item is the one which is already admitted, so we'll give numbers for the number 2, 3, and 4. So 12193 will be admitted as Exhibit P?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 2485; 1D8455 will be Exhibit D2486; 1D8456 will be Exhibit D2487.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And 1D8458?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will be Exhibit D2489, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to read out the summary of Mr. Kovacevic's statement in English. [In English] Zoran Kovacevic was mobilised on 8th of May, 1992, as an ordinary private into the ranks of Vogosca Brigade in an infantry unit for the protection of the explosive stores in the Pretis special purpose production company. In the second half of 1992, he was transferred to the Artillery Unit. In mid 1993, he went to Banja Luka to complete officer training where he gained the rank of 2nd Lieutenant. On 28th of June, 1994, he entered the 16th Krajina Motorised Brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps. After that, in late 1994 or early 1995, he returned to the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade as an artillery support battalion commander. In March 1992, Zoran Kovacevic saw armed Muslim paramilitary units riding Volkswagen vans with revolving lights, wearing green and dark red berets. The object of his unit's interest was the Zuc facility which was located between Serb and Muslim units and the city and it -- it was the enemy's units located -- where they have been located. His understanding of the strategy and the objective which the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps laid down was regard -- with regard to the city of Sarajevo were of a defensive nature. Neither he nor his unit understood those actions to be part of a systematic or widespread attack on civilians. He had knowledge that the objective of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command was to block the forces of the 1st Corps of the BH in the city in order to prevent their exit and use on other fronts in BH. This breakthrough would have had negative consequences for the VRS on the remaining fronts and the course of the war in BH. The BH 1st Corps army -- 1st Corps was in the city of Sarajevo under the control of the Muslim authorities in the period from April 1992 to December 1995. The units of the 1st Corps of BH Army opposed to him -- his unit were 111th, 112th, and 105th Mountain Brigades which held the dominant points of Zuc, Orlic, Hum, Grdonj, Brijesce Brdo, and Sokolje. They also had positions in civilian zones including mortars stationed in the Sarajevo maternity hospital. They also mounted multi-rocket launchers on vehicles and modified anti-aircraft defence weapons for fire against ground targets. His unit had knowledge that there were military targets behind the lines. His unit took precautionary measures to avoid firing on civilian facilities located in the zone of responsibility of the 1st BH army corps and to reduce collateral civilian casualties. In addition to this, his unit on more than one occasion abandoned combat or fire operations because of the disproportionate danger of civilian casualties in relation to the military objective to be achieved. He had no knowledge that any casualties of battle were civilians. Neither he nor members of his unit or higher or lower commands had any intention to cause civilian casualties in the part of the city under Muslim control or accomplish psychological impact or conduct a campaign of terror against them. He was never ordered either verbally or in writing by higher command or civilian authorities to carry out attacks on civilians of public transportations in the part of the city under Muslim control, nor did he ever issue such orders. On the contrary, instructions received from the higher command or civilian authorities were that the fire should be open exclusively at military targets threatening their forces. Verbal orders from superior command, as well as those issued by Zoran Kovacevic to his subordinates stated that civilians in the city under Muslim control must not be the target of an attack. His unit's crews were not fully manned. Its members were not professional soldiers but reserves. That means local people and the unit's command staff was not comprised of professional officers either. The ammunition situation in his unit varied, but as time went on ammunition became scarcer and were forced to turn to war time production ammunition. Orders from the higher command regarding the expenditure, especially of artillery ammunition, prescribed that it had to be used sparingly. Squandering of the ammunition was not allowed. He had knowledge of the existence of manufactured -- manufacture of modified aerial bombs for firing on ground targets due to the shortage of -- a shortage of the classic artillery ammunition, while in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps there were aerial bombs that were unused because of the no-fly order that was in place. Regarding incident Markale I on 5th of February, 1994, Zoran Kovacevic states that to his knowledge, there were no artillery units or mortars on that axis. Secondly, knowing the configuration of the market and the distance from the possible firing point on that axis, he considers the possibility of a hit on that spot to be minimal and that it borders on the impossible. Regarding incident at Dositejeva Street 4A on 16 of June, 1995, to Zoran Kovacevic's knowledge, nobody from Pretis or his brigade launched an aerial bomb on 16th of June, 1995, at Dositejeva Street. [Interpretation] Thank you. During examination-in-chief, I would kindly ask that the witness be provided a hard copy in Serbian, perhaps the one I have in my hand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you to read out paragraph number 5 for your own sake. You don't have to do it out loud. I just want you to be acquainted with its contents. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at 1D8457 next. Did you read the entire paragraph, because it goes on to page 2.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in, please. Could we focus on the circle which delineates the 20-kilometre perimeter. The picture's not the best, but did you make certain markings on the map?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can barely see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see red markings, squares, rectangles, to the north of Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can see three such shapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain the Chamber what the circles is and what the markings stand for regarding paragraph 5 which you read.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The red shapes probably depict firing positions, and the circle, inside the circle we have the city area of Sarajevo with its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the witness could be assisted in marking Dobrinja -- sorry, Vogosca, and then the hills between Vogosca and the city, and I would like him to mark Zuc on the map as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This should be Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mark it with a V.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the range of hills you marked, what is that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's the general area of the Hum and Zuc features.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you put a Z with a diacritic and an H.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can one see the central part of the city to the south of Zuc and Hum from Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. There is no line of sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the positions refers to in paragraph 5, can you tell us what was their position on the map?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They were turned towards Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the positions have to do with the howitzer battery that is mentioned in paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I also ask you to place a date and your initials in the lower right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Today's date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Another thing, perhaps I'm asking much, but can you depict the axis towards Dositejeva Street and what would be the distance approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I have no idea where Dositejeva Street would be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, it's quite far to the centre of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this. Perhaps it could be under the same number with the markings, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted as the next Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2488, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the Prosecution -- Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, two or three short questions as part of my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see no problem. Please continue then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, what was the ethnic make-up of your brigade? Were there people of other ethnicities in your brigade, and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the various brigade units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How about your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In my artillery battalion there were Croats and Bosniaks or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If the Serbs were obliged to respond to call-ups, were Croats and Muslims obliged to do the same or were they mobilised by force?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Members of other ethnicities also volunteered to the unit and they were made part of it. They had never been officially mobilised though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So at first they were volunteers, but did they enjoy the same status as VRS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. They were members of the VRS, and all VRS members enjoyed the same rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the fact that you had artillery pieces, did you have observation points and where?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Our observation points were for a while at the firing lines while at other times we used forward observation points at the lines held by the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you in communication with them, with the people at the observation posts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the same situation in place throughout the war when you returned to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. At this stage I have no more questions of Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, thank you for meeting briefly with myself and an investigator on Monday. I hope we will be able to move through the examination efficiently. I would ask you to focus on the question and answer the question that I put, because we are limited in time. I only have one hour to put some questions to you. You said on Monday that you were mobilised -- when you were mobilised in May 1992, you were part of a platoon of 25 to 30 men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Sutherland speak into the microphone right in front of her. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say it was a 25- to 30-member detachment. Oh, you mean the infantry unit. Yes, that unit numbered 20 to 30 men. The unit that was the protective platoon for the ammunitions depot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And two or three months later you transferred to the artillery unit of the Vogosca Brigade and Zeljko Blavacenin [phoen] was the artillery unit commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He reported to the brigade's chief of artillery Sretko [phoen] Gracanin. And Gracanin's superior was Trifunovic, the Vogosca Brigade commander, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You left the area to go to Banja Luka for officer training around the 1st of September, 1993, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's about right. It wasn't really training. It was an officer school of the VRS. There is a difference between training and education.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said when you returned to the area in late 1994, early 1995, that you were made commander of the mixed artillery battalion of the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade which was formally known as the Vogosca Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Gracanin was still the brigade's chief of artillery and his superior was the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about the type and number of artillery weapons you had in the period 1992 to mid-1993. You had artillery positions at Krivoglavci, Blagovac, Hotonj, and Gradacac. What type and calibre of the two howitzer did you have at the Blagovac position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: One howitzer, 105 millimetre; and a 122-millimetre howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So besides the weapons that you mention in your statement in paragraph 4 and the one that you just mentioned now, or, the two that you mention now, the 105 millimetre and the 122 millimetre, the brigade also had a number of other weapons, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You had 128-millimetre Plamen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is a 128-millimetre Plamen, and I heard a Praga, which is not the case. It's not Praga. It's 128-millimetre Plamen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's what I -- that's what I said. It was obviously -- I didn't speak clearly enough. You also had 155-million howitzers in Tihovici [phoen] and Zemina Ravan [phoen] and in Kremes, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please repeat the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... the interpretation. We had 122-millimetre howitzers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also had 155-millimetre howitzers in Tihovici, Zemina Ravan and in Kremes, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, those were not the positions in 1992, the ones you referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was talking about the period 1992 through 'til 1993, September, when you went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: There was a howitzer battery, a 122-millimetre howitzer battery at Kremes. 120-millimetre mortars at Krivoglavci, Blagovac, and Hotonj. A 76-millimetre gun, B-1, at Gradac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What about a 76-millimetre gun, ZiS 3, Z-i-s 3, in Blagovac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: A 76-million ZiS gun. I believe there was one in Hotonj but it didn't belong to my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But Hotonj was part of the Vogosca Brigade, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But not all artillery belonged to my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At the moment I'm asking you about what the brigade had. What about 122-millimetre howitzer D-30 in Zimena Ravan?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: A 122-millimetre D-30 howitzer was at Blagovac. So there were two howitzers, a 105 millimetre and a 122 millimetre D-30 howitzer. They were the Blagovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. The brigade are also had -- or the Artillery Unit that you were in also had a tank T-55 and a Praga, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's not artillery. A tank is an armoured mechanised asset, a Praga is an anti-aircraft asset, so these are not land artillery pieces and this could not have been part -- within my unit; within the brigade, yes, but not in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're right. You're absolutely right. Sorry. I -- I -- I should have said to you: You had within your Artillery Unit drivers for these vehicles, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Vehicle drivers. Well, they would be within those units that service them. These were drivers of special combat vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. And in 1995, did you have any other artillery weapons that you haven't already mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: A howitzer battery, a 122-millimetre howitzer battery at Kremes; a 105-howitzer battery - I can't say exactly in what sector they were. In the background of Rajlovac some place - then there was a B-1 battery at Krivoglavci; one Plamen VBR; one Oganj VBR, and that would be about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 12191. Mr. Kovacevic, this is a list of persons in the artillery section, and we see that you're listed at number 2.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] under. The document is undated, but if we go to the last page we can see that it's signed by Robert Jovanovski. When did Jovanovski take over as the commander of the Sarajevo 3rd Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but that wasn't the 3rd Infantry Brigade, the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade but, rather, the Vogosca Brigade. That's as far as the brigade is concerned. Now, Robert Jovanovski took over from Miladin Trifunovic. This was, as far as I recall, in 1992, perhaps the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Or at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we see here that there are drivers for the Pragas and the T-55 tanks.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that, but could we see the top of this document or, rather, the first page. This is a list of conscripts in artillery. Now, at this time, the word artillery comprised everything. In other words, whatever was in the artillery battalion and then also what was in the light rocket and anti-aircraft battalion, and in the armoured mechanised unit. So this is an overall list probably for rations of cigarettes or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P6013, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you mention in your statement that you had a 120-millimetre M-38 howitzer, and in fact you've just testified today about the Blagovac Battalion having -- or, at their artillery position having a D-30 howitzer. There's quite a -- there's a difference in the ranges between those two weapons, is there not? The M-38 has a range of 11.800 metres, while the D-30 has a range of approximately 15.300 metres.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, but this is not a 120-millimetre howitzer but rather a 122-millimetre M-38 howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I misspoke if I said 128. I meant 122. But you agree with me, don't you? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you mean the range, yes. These are the technical specifications for those weapons, and it's correct. One of them has a slightly shorter range and the other one longer, and of course these figures approximately are correct, 11.800 and 15.300.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And also you said in your statement that -- that you had a 76-millimetre old gun, an M-48(B-1) and then you mentioned today that you had the more powerful 76-millimetre ZiS-3 gun at Blagovac and there's a quite a difference between these two guns is there not? The M-48 has a range of 8.750 metres, and the ZiS-3 has a range of 13.000 metres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that the range of ZiS is 13.000 metres, but that asset was not with me. What I had was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the weapon, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the range, it is correct. With D-1 it's 8.750 or something. As for ZiS, I don't really know. That's an anti-armour asset.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the weapon you were first referring to. That was the M-48, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned also that the brigade had multiple-rocket launchers. This is an anti- -- an area anti-personnel weapon not suitable for point targeting in urban environment because its range of error is too great, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Multiple-rocket launchers are not anti-aircraft assets. Multiple-rocket launchers are --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Anti-personnel. Anti-personnel.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Those are multiple-rocket launchers. That's -- that's land rocket artillery which implies that they can be used against targets on the ground. They're not -- it's not an anti-aircraft weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. I said -- I'm sorry. It must have been a mistranslation. I said anti-personnel weapon. So you agree that it's a land -- to be -- to be used on the ground. It's also right, isn't it, that the range of error is -- is -- is quite large?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "range of error."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's not -- it's not precise.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It is precise as specified according to the technical specifications. These are multiple-rocket launchers used to target targets on the ground. I can't say they're not precise. It depends on the target. It is true that it is an area weapon, and in that sense it should be rather precise. I don't know how to put this. It's not a rifle so that you can pinpoint a target. Artillery weapons are different. They have a breadth, a width, a depth, an azimuth, and so on, so they are defined according to several parameters. These are multidimensional targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: During the two time periods that you were there, 1992 through 'til September 1993 and then again late 1994, beginning of 1995 until the end of the war, did the artillery positions remain the same?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They remained more or less the same perhaps with some slight adjustments, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what do you mean by some slight adjustments?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps they were moved by a hundred, 200 metres along the line, the front line, because -- well, we had a defence line behind our backs, and this was the only artillery that we had at our disposal so that sometimes it had to be turned against the outer ring. So practically we operated in semi -- in a semi-surrounding position. We were turned -- we had positions towards the town but also behind our backs. So the territory -- our territory there was very narrow, perhaps 3 to 4 or 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And during the -- the two time periods that we just talked about, did the weaponry stay at the locations you've mentioned in your statement throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At the locations that I mentioned in my statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many 122-millimetre howitzers did the unit -- did the brigade have in 1995? The brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, toward the end of 1995, I believe that there were four of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mean the 122-millimetre D-30s or all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: All 122-millimetre weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And let's say in -- in May, May 1995.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly about May 1995, but at the end of 1995 there were probably six to eight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so we've just gone through quite a number of additional weapons that -- that the -- that -- that your unit had and the brigade had. Why did you minimise the holdings of the artillery in your -- in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In my statement, I did not even mention the number of weapons. I only mentioned howitzer battery.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm talking about the types of weapons. We've just gone through quite a number of additional weapons that -- that you had. Many?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see what additional weapons. There was that 122-millimetre calibre, 105, 76, VBR, Oganj. I don't know what's additional.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The different types of 76-millimetre guns, the fact that 122-millimetre hasn't been mentioned in your statement at all.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I did mention 122-millimetre weapons in my statement, but here it says 120-millimetres M-38, but I said 122 millimetres. Here it says 120 M-38.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move on now to -- you mentioned that orders came from higher command levels regarding the expenditure of ammunition especially artillery, that it must be used sparingly. Did you mean that an order came from the corps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All orders came from higher commanders. In other words, we received orders from higher commands and the orders on the expenditure of ammunition was they had to be used sparingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so the brigades had to change their attitude towards the way artillery was being used. What needed to be changed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The expenditure of ammunition should be minimised. That was received at the brigade. And then from the brigade I received an order, an order for operation. And there was nothing for me to think about as far as the expenditure of ammunition was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as part of that order -- or did -- did the -- did the brigades have to submit daily ammunition expenditure reports to the SRK command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If you believe me, I don't know. The brigade was my superior command, and I received my order from them, whereas the brigade would report to their superior command. I believe that was the way it should be, but I don't really know. I had no insight into how the brigade operated, nor was it necessary for me to have that kind of insight.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [In English] I shouldn't rather than it was necessary. [Interpretation] May I intervene in the transcript. The witness said I should rather than it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, what wasn't necessary? What did you say was necessary?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Because that was the superior command. What the -- what the superior command did, that wasn't something that I had to know. I didn't have to know about that. That's how the military structure functions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But you were advised by the -- the command through the brigade that -- that artillery was being squandered because it was often fired are --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you receiving it now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, now I hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But you were informed by the command through the brigade that the reason that ammunition was being squandered was because it was being fired at inhabited settlements and specific buildings when there was no combat action whatsoever; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That is not right. The corps command had nothing to tell me. They would relate it to the brigade, and the brigade received orders that they should not squander ammunition, but what you've just mentioned, that's rather broad. So that's not how it was. We were to prevent squandering of ammunition and to spare -- use it sparingly, because we didn't -- there wasn't much of it. But the context in which you put it, that's not -- that was not the reason why ammunition was to be used sparingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I thought you said that the -- the -- the order that came down from the corps command was then -- that order was passed on to your brigade, was it not, down through the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. An order came to the effect that we have to use ammunition sparingly, but not for the reasons that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can quickly have P2668, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, this is -- this is the order from General Milosevic, and if you can see the second -- second paragraph there. Does this refresh your memory as to the order that came down from the corps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This is an order from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command sent to and then it says there who it was sent to, to brigade commands. This is the first time ever that I see this order. And I wasn't even supposed to see this. This was an order sent to the brigade from the superior command -- or, rather, it was sent to the brigade which was my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. I will move on. In paragraph 12 of your statement, you said that you had knowledge of military targets behind the lines, the command post communication centres, artillery and mortar, and you said: "Despite this, during the conduct of combat and fire operations against military targets located in civilian zones, we took measures to reduce collateral civilian casualties ..." How do you reconcile that with what you state in paragraph 10, and I quote: "There was no uncertainty in myself or my unit during conduct of combat or fire operations as to whether operations or fire were being directed towards civilians. In other words, we/I never accepted such a possibility and continued fire despite this."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I understood all the rest surrounding it, as it were, but could you repeat the question itself, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, you're saying on the one hand that you took precautionary measures to reduce collateral civilian casualties, but earlier on in your statement you say there was no uncertainty as to whether operations of fire were being directed towards civilians, and you never accepted such a possibility and you continued to fire despite it. So I'm just -- how do you reconcile those two -- two statements?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that despite everything I continued opening fire. As for what the statement says, it means the following: Civilians were not the target of the artillery units, my artillery. Civilians were not the targets of the operation of the artillery units. As for paragraph 12, the enemy units were often positioned in civilian buildings and facilities where civilians moved about. I said that these were artillery --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness will have to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Kovacevic, interpreters are saying to ask that you are speaking a bit too fast. Could you slow down and repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. So military targets in terms of the deployment of enemy forces was such that they were positioned in civilian locations. So these were their staffs, communication centres, artillery positions, their mobile mortars, their mobile multiple-rocket launchers, and that is why I said that despite all of that -- that despite all of that, we did not open fire at military targets located in civilian zones. Or if that was necessary, we took all measures to diminish or reduce collateral civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But what you say in your statement was that -- is that the three BiH Army units opposing you all positions in civilian zones. That's what you say in paragraph 8. And so then if you are responding to fire from those units, then you are firing back into civilian zones, are you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. Military zones. If you put a tank somewhere, that's a military target.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've said in paragraph 8 that -- that -- first of all, you say in paragraph 7 that you are responding -- you're responding to fire from the city, and you say in paragraph 11 that you received verbal orders that civilians in the city weren't to be the target. Are you talking about -- are you talking about returning fire on the positions that opened fire on your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As far as the zone of operation of my unit is concerned, the city had nothing to do with that. I said at the very outset it was the Zuc feature, Zuc. As far as fire from the city was concerned, and there was such fire, that fire was opened at the municipality of Vogosca practically every day. We did not respond to that fire, the fire coming from the urban zones, because that goes beyond the area of responsibility of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why did you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The area of responsibility is Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, but in your statement in paragraph 7 you say: "... when conducting combat operations, firing or responding to fire from the city." So you're talking here about responding to fire in the city.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Fire in town? I cannot see that now, but I personally and my unit when opening fire carrying out combat operations, we did not understand that as part of a systematic or widespread attack on civilians. We did not respond to fire from the city of Sarajevo. The zone of responsibility of my unit is Zuc and what I've already mentioned. So it is the broader area of Zuc. The city was not within the area of responsibility of my brigade. Rather, it was the feature of Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And on the map earlier today you drew a circle which went right down to -- to the -- to the city, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. To the city itself but not into the city, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you said you've never had any knowledge that there were any civilian casualties during the war. Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I did not have such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Never once a commander ever said to you that despite all these precautions that you -- that it wasn't working and that civilians in Sarajevo were being killed and injured?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. The commander never said that to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As far as Sarajevo was concerned -- sorry. Once again you're talking about Sarajevo. The zone of operation is the hill of Zuc. That is where the enemy's front end was. Sarajevo for me was the depth. The city of Sarajevo, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You just said the hill of Zuc, but you said a moment ago -- or you said in your statement that -- that the BiH units opposing you all had positions in civilian zones. So where were the civilian zones in Zuc? If you're now saying it's the hill.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A hill is a geographic feature that can be populated. As far as Zuc is concerned, it's mostly Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that your commander never once said, but did you hear from anybody that there was ever any civilians killed or wounded during operations, your combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You didn't hear about any people being taken from the detention facilities in Vogosca to work on Zuc who were killed and wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You agree that the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade is in the north-western part of the front; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you purport to have absolutely no knowledge at all on the technical details of the workings of a modified air-bomb.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said you have --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say no knowledge. I said that I did have some knowledge, that I heard about that, but as for knowledge concerning operations, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said you have some knowledge on the existence of a manufacture of modified aerial bombs which the SRK had in its arsenal. Is that the knowledge you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is what I heard. It wasn't official. I heard that that existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
